title: An Anti-Inflammatory Diet Can Cut Dementia Risk by Nearly a Third — Even After Alzheimer's Has Begun in Your Brain
excerpt: A 15-year study of nearly 1,900 older adults found that eating foods rich in antioxidants and healthy fats lowered dementia rates by up to 29 percent, even in people whose blood already carried elevated Alzheimer's biomarkers — and the traditional Indian pantry is a natural fit.
body:
Alzheimer's disease does not announce itself with a single dramatic moment. It builds silently for years, laying down plaques and tangles in the brain long before a person forgets a name or misplaces a set of keys. Scientists have known this for decades. What they have struggled to answer is whether anything done during that silent buildup can actually change the outcome.

A study published this week in *JAMA Network Open* offers one of the clearest answers yet — and the prescription is remarkably ordinary. Researchers from the University of Ljubljana tracked nearly 1,900 Swedish adults aged 60 and older for 15 years, measuring what they ate, testing their blood for early Alzheimer's warning signals, and watching who eventually developed dementia. The results were striking: people who consistently followed an anti-inflammatory diet were significantly less likely to develop cognitive decline, and the benefit was most pronounced among those whose biology suggested they were already at heightened risk.

The team, led by researcher Anja Mrhar, measured three blood-based biomarkers that scientists increasingly use as early signals of neurodegeneration. Phosphorylated tau (p-tau) is associated with the protein tangles that define Alzheimer's pathology. Neurofilament light chain (NfL) reflects active damage to nerve cells. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) rises when the brain's support cells are responding to injury. Elevated levels of any of these markers suggest that harmful changes may already be underway — even in people who feel cognitively normal.

Among people with high tau levels, those who ate more anti-inflammatory foods had a 29 percent lower risk of developing dementia. The reduction was 21 percent for those with elevated NfL, and 27 percent among those with raised GFAP levels. In other words, eating well appeared to offer a degree of protection even after the biological machinery of Alzheimer's had begun to turn.

## What Counts as Anti-Inflammatory?



> **"Phosphorylated tau (p-tau) is associated with the protein tangles that define Alzheimer's pathology."**


The study did not require participants to follow any branded diet plan. Instead, it scored their overall eating patterns on a scale of how pro- or anti-inflammatory their food choices were. The foods that scored well are familiar to anyone who has read about the Mediterranean or DASH diets: colourful fruits and vegetables, berries, leafy greens, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, olive oil, and fatty fish. The foods that scored poorly — processed snacks, refined sugars, excessive red meat, and foods high in saturated and trans fats — are equally unsurprising.


![University of Ljubljana — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/University_of_Ljubljana_Palace.jpg/3840px-University_of_Ljubljana_Palace.jpg)


What makes these findings particularly relevant for the Indian diaspora is that many of the foods at the heart of an anti-inflammatory pattern are already staples of traditional South Asian cuisine. Turmeric, whose active compound curcumin has demonstrated anti-inflammatory properties across dozens of studies, is used almost daily in Indian cooking. Lentils, chickpeas, spinach, tomatoes, ginger, garlic, and a wide array of spices — fenugreek, coriander, cinnamon — all carry anti-inflammatory or antioxidant profiles. A thali built around dal, sabzi, roti, and raita is, by default, closer to what this study's protective diet looks like than a typical Western plate.

## The Diaspora Paradox

The challenge for NRIs and second-generation South Asians is that migration often nudges eating patterns in the wrong direction. The convenience of processed foods, the social pull of fast-food culture, and the sheer pace of life in Western cities can gradually erode a diet that was naturally protective. Studies have repeatedly shown that South Asians in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada have higher rates of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome than their counterparts in India — conditions that are themselves risk factors for dementia.

This study adds another dimension to that picture. Chronic low-grade inflammation, driven in part by diet, appears to accelerate the very brain changes that lead to Alzheimer's. And the protective effect of anti-inflammatory eating is not just preventive — it appears to slow the process even after it has begun.

## What This Means in Practice

The study is observational, meaning it cannot prove that diet alone caused the lower dementia rates. People who eat well often exercise more, sleep better, and manage their blood pressure more carefully, and these factors likely contributed too. But the 15-year follow-up period, the inclusion of blood biomarkers, and the consistency of the results with a large body of prior evidence give the findings considerable weight.

For diaspora Indians navigating the competing demands of two food cultures, the takeaway is encouraging: the traditional foods many grew up eating may be among the most powerful tools available for long-term brain protection. The key is not adopting an exotic new diet, but preserving — or returning to — one that your grandmother already knew.

**Sources:** *JAMA Network Open* (University of Ljubljana, 2026); Alzheimer's Association; National Institute on Aging.
